# A year-end spending rush in FY2026? Five tests, against FY2023-FY2025

<!-- GENERATED by scripts/build_year_end_rush.py from sources/data/munis-school-journal.csv. Do not edit by hand; --check fails if this file no longer reproduces. -->

Scope: the school general fund (fund 0100, department 300), the lines that make up the reported leftover. Window: 15 May to 30 June. FY2026 has not been closed in this run of the journal, so its open orders can still move.

## What the data shows

- **Next year's bills paid early: $189,276.75 in FY2026, nothing in the three years before.** Nine collaborative tuition invoices numbered for FY2027 were charged to FY2026 on 30 June. Without them FY2026 would have reported $671,395 left, not $482,118.07.
- **Late orders: 17.4% of FY2026's discretionary orders, by final value, were opened after 15 May** ($323,648). In the three years before: FY2023 9.0%, FY2024 17.0%, FY2025 10.0%. So FY2026 ordered late at about the pace of FY2024, and about twice the pace of FY2023 and FY2025. Against the three-year pattern that is $56,004 more than usual (our estimate, method below).
- **June payments: 20.9% of FY2026's discretionary invoices were paid in June ($365,181), more than in any of the three years before (FY2023 13.8%, FY2024 15.9%, FY2025 13.2%).** $240,199 of it is dated 30 June. The three largest orders opened after 15 May were Chromebooks, $135,000 together, ordered 10 and 25 June (test 1).
- **Orders still open at 30 June: $53,242 on discretionary lines in FY2026**, against $14,570, $163,132 and $43,641 in the three years before; $32,295 of it ordered after 15 May.
- **The other way: $333,494.89 of collaborative tuition was moved off the general fund onto the circuit breaker on 29 June 2026.** Without that entry the leftover would have been smaller by the same amount. It is shown separately below and never netted in.

## The leftover before the late spending

Reported leftover is what each year left unspent and uncommitted, counted the FY2026 way in every year (orders still open at the close subtracted), from `fy_breakdown.py`. The layers above it are added back.

| | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Leftover as reported | $32,022 | $31,705 | $554,945 | $482,118.07 |
| + next year's bills charged to this year (measured) | -- | -- | -- | $189,276.75 |
| + late discretionary spending above the usual (**our estimate**) | -$106,530 | $127,889 | -$45,542 | $56,004 |
| **= leftover before the late spending (our estimate)** | **-$74,508** | **$159,594** | **$509,403** | **$727,399** |
| *separately: charged to the circuit breaker instead, 29 June* | -- | -- | -- | $333,494.89 |

**How the "above the usual" line is estimated (ours).** For each discretionary group, the ratio is orders opened 15 May-30 June over orders opened before 15 May, each at its final value in the year (opened, plus later changes and cancellations), pooled across the OTHER baseline years (FY2026 is compared with FY2023-FY2025; each baseline year with the other two). That ratio, applied to the year's own early orders, is the late ordering the year would have had at the usual pace; the line is the actual late orders less that. A negative figure means less than usual. The baseline is only three years and one of them (FY2024) ordered late at the FY2026 pace, so the estimate is sensitive to which years are in it. Open orders at 30 June are not a third layer: a late order still open is already in this line. Invoices paid with no order, and journal entries moving costs onto grants, are not in it.

## What it does not show

- **Why.** Nothing in the journal records the reason for an order. A late order can be a rush to use money before it lapses, a purchase planned for the summer when buildings are empty, a delayed delivery, or an order held until the year's tuition and special education costs were known. The data cannot tell these apart.
- **What was bought, or whether it was needed.** The journal gives a vendor, an account and an eighteen-character description. Registered as a gap: *What a purchase ordered in the last six weeks of a school year was for* (`money-gaps.csv`).
- **The size of any deficit.** Nothing here measures a deficit in FY2026 or FY2027. It measures when money was committed.
- **FY2026 is not closed.** Its open orders, and so its leftover, can still move at the close.

## A possible explanation, offered as a hypothesis

TJ was told there was a "mad dash of spending" at the FY2026 year end because of a large deficit. Two readings of "deficit" lead to two different hypotheses, and the tests bear on them differently:

1. **A rush to spend a leftover before it lapses.** Unspent general fund money returns to the town at the close. If this were the cause, late discretionary orders would run above the usual pace. What the tests found: FY2026 ordered late at about twice the pace of FY2023 and FY2025 but at the pace of FY2024, and paid a larger share of its invoices in June than any of the three. Consistent with a rush; also consistent with FY2024's pattern recurring, and the three-year baseline cannot separate the two.
2. **Prepaying a short year.** The district's FY2027 balanced proposal was $761,000 below its level-service proposal (`budget-workbooks/fy27-proposals.xlsx`, sheet `FY27 Budget Projection`, `L404` = $27,333,288.00 Level Service Proposed, `M404` = $26,572,287.50 Balanced Proposed). If this were the cause, FY2027 costs would be charged to FY2026 money. What the tests found: one instance of that shape, $189,276.75 of FLLAC tuition numbered for FY2027, and none in the three years before. It is the largest layer in the bridge. Whether it was paid early to ease FY2027, or because the invoices arrived then, nothing here says.

Nothing here establishes either motive. The timing is measured; the reason is not. What would settle it: the purchase orders opened after 15 May 2026 with their requisitions and approvals, and FLLAC's invoices `27L2KEY11`-`27L2KEY19` with their service dates.
